paras: The killing of Allen Chapman was the shooting of a Black man by a band of masked, armed men at his cabin in Haywood district, Chattooga County, Georgia, on the night of about June 6, 1881. The band had come for a white girl who lived with him, and when Chapman met them with a shotgun they opened fire; he was reported dead. A Columbus dispatch carried in the Wheeling Intelligencer under the headline "Murder by Georgia Regulators" is the only known report.

According to the dispatch, Chapman, "a colored man," had been living in the same cabin with "a very comely girl of pure white blood," and this had caused "considerable excitement" in the district for some time. Anonymous warnings had been sent to both of them several times that there would be "trouble" if they continued to live together. The warnings went unheeded, and the dispatch spoke of "ominous mutterings of a disturbance."

On the night before the June 7 dispatch, a band of masked and armed men appeared at Chapman's door and demanded the girl. Chapman came to the door instead, armed with a shotgun, and the band at once fired on him, filling his body with shot, and then withdrew. He was described as "horribly wounded" and "now reported dead," so the dispatch reported his death without confirming it. The dispatch names none of the attackers, gives no number for the band, and says nothing of what became of the girl.
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The story reached print in a short Columbus, Georgia, dispatch on the front page of the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer in West Virginia on June 8, 1881; no Georgia paper's account was found. Its headline called the shooting "Murder" and the attackers "Georgia Regulators," yet the body of the dispatch dwelt on the couple's living arrangement, the girl's "pure white blood" and the ignored warnings, presenting the attack as the outcome of local feeling. The dispatch spelled the victim's name "Chapmen" at first mention and "Chapman" afterward.
